INTRODUCTION 
 
 I, the Chairperson, Standing Committee on Chemicals and Fertilizers  
 (2025-26) having been authorized by the Committee, do present on their behalf this  
Twenty-fifth Report on Action Taken by the Government on the Observations/Recommendations 
contained in the Fifteenth Report of the Standing Committee on Chemicals and Fertilizers (Eighteenth 
Lok Sabha) on ‘Self-sufficiency in production of fertilizers with a view to curb import of fertilizers — review 
of constraints thereof’, pertaining to the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers (Department of Fertilizers). 
2.  The Fifteenth Report was presented to  Hon’ble Speaker, Lok Sabha on 4 th October, 2025, 
presented to Lok Sabha on 1 st December, 2025 and laid in Rajya Sabha on 21 st August, 2025. The 
Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Department of Fertilizers, furnished their replies in 23rd February, 
2026 indicating Action Taken on the Observations/Recommendations contained in the Fifteenth Report. 
The Committee considered and adopted this Report at their Sitting held on 29th June, 2026. 
3. An analysis of the Action Taken by the Government on the Observations/Recommendations 
contained in the Fifteenth Report (Eighteenth Lok Sabha) of the Committee is given in Appendix-II. 
4. For ease of reference, Observations/Recommendations of the Committee have been printed in 
bold letters in the Report. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
New Delhi;                                                                                                      Azad Kirti Jha 
29 June, 2026                                                                                             Chairperson, 
08 Ashadha, 1948 (Saka)                                                                             Standing Committee on 
     Chemicals and Fertilizers 
  
 
  

 1 
 
REPORT 
CHAPTER – I 
This Report deals with the action taken by the Government on the 
Observations/Recommendations contained in the Fifteenth Report (1 8th Lok 
Sabha) of the Committee on 'Self-sufficiency in production of fertilizers with a 
view to curb import of fertilizers — review of constraints thereof’, pertaining to the 
Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers (Department of Fertilizers).  
1.2  The Fifteenth Report was presented to Lok Sabha and laid in Rajya Sabha 
on 25.07.2025. It contained 31 Observations / Recommendations. Replies of the 
Government in respect of all the recommendations have been received and are 
categorized as follows: 
(i)  Observations/Recommendations which have been accepted 
by the Government (Chapter II): 
Rec. Sl. No. 1, 3, 6, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 18, 20, 22, 23, 24, 26, 28, 29, 
30 and 31                  (Total =19) 
(ii)  Observations/Recommendations which the Committee do not 
desire to pursue in view of the Government’s reply (Chapter III): 
Rec. Sl. No. 15, 17, 19, 21 and 27                (Total-05)                                         
(iii)  Observations/Recommendations in respect of which replies of 
the Government have not been accepted by the Committee (Chapter 
IV):  
Rec. Sl. No. 4, 5, 9 and 25                                                      (Total-04)     
 (iv)  Observations/Recommendations in respect of which final 
replies of the Government are of interim nature (Chapter V): 
           Rec. Sl. No. 2, 7 and 10                                              (Total-03)
  
1.3 The Committee desire that the Action Taken Notes on the 
Observations / Recommendations contained in Chapter-I of this Report and 
the final replies in respect of Observations/Recommendations contained in 
Chapter IV for which interim reply has been furnished by the Ministry may 
be furnished to them at the earliest.  

 2 
 
1.4 The Committee will now deal with some of their earlier 
Observations/Recommendations which either require reiteration or merit further 
comments. 
RECOMMENDATION SL. No. 4 
 
 Revival of Closed Units of FCIL and HFCL 
1.5  Noting the status of revival of closed units of Fertilizer Corporation of India 
Ltd. (FCIL) and Hindustan Fertilizers Corporation Ltd. (HFCL) aimed at 
augmenting domestic urea production, the Committee recommended as under: - 
        “The Committee find that five units of Fertilizer Corporation of India Ltd 
(FCIL) at Sindri (Jharkhand), Talcher (Odisha), Ramagundam (Telangana), 
Gorakhpur (Uttar Pradesh) and Korba (Chhattisgarh) and three units of 
Hindustan Fertilizers Corporation Ltd (HFCL)  at Durgapur, Haldia (both in West 
Bengal) and Barauni (Bihar) were closed down since September, 2002 due to 
obsolete technology and high energy consumption of plants and economic 
unviability. However, to increase Urea production in the Country, the 
Government, approved revival of Talcher and Ramagundam units of FCIL in 
2011 by setting up gas-based fertilizer plants of 1.27 MMTPA capacity.  Further, 
the Government, in Year 2016, approved revival of Gorakhpur & Sindri units of 
FCIL and Barauni unit of HFCL b y setting up gas -based fertilizer plants of 1.27 
MMTPA capacity each. The Committee are happy to note that the Ramagundam, 
Gorakhpur, Barauni and Sindri fertilizer plants have started urea production 
whereas the Talcher plant is under execution phase.  The Committee, further find 
that the Talcher project was being set up as a greenfield urea plant through coal 
gasification technology, utilizing the abundantly available domestic coal for Urea 
production. Statedly, on completion of the project, the production  of urea in the 
Country will increase and it will also provide security in feedstock supply as coal 
would be sourced domestically and provide alternate route for urea production. 
The Committee note that against the urea consumption of 388 LMT, the 
indigenous production of Urea was 307 LMT during 2024 -25 and the demand is 
expected to increase to 444 LMT by 2035 -36. With a view to enhance the Urea 
production in the Country and achieve self -reliance in its production, the 
Committee, strongly, recommends for ta king timely effective policy initiatives to 
facilitate early revival of Durgapur and Haldia units of HFCL and Korba unit of 
FCIL by leveraging their strategic locations and existing infrastructure, and 
utilizing the coal-gasification route, etc. which woul d reduce the demand supply 
gap of urea and enhance domestic production capacity. The Committee would 
like to be apprised of the progress made by the Department in this regard.” 
 

 3 
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT 
1.6  In their action taken reply to the afore -mentioned recommendation of 
the Committee, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Department of 
Fertilizers has stated as under: - 
“Government of India mandated revival of Ramagundam (Telangana), 
Gorakhpur (Uttar Pradesh), Sindri (Jharkhand) and Talcher (Odisha) units of 
Fertilizer Corporation of India and Barauni (Bihar) unit of Hindustan Fertilizer 
Corporation Limited through Joint V enture Company of nominated PSUs for 
setting up new ammonia -urea plants of 12.7 LMTPA capacity each. The 
revival of Talcher unit of FCIL is under execution stage and after 
operationalization of Talcher unit, a total of 63.5 LMTPA of domestic 
production wo uld be added.  In addition, a new fertilizer plant at Namrup, 
Assam of 12.7 LMTPA capacity has been approved and JV agreement 
signed. Therefore, decision on revival of other units of FCIL and HFCL would 
be taken based on the demand supply gap of urea after  operationalization of 
all these plants.  
 It is mentioned that the previous submissions to the Standing 
Committee included land details and revival possibilities for Haldia and 
Durgapur plants vide Department of Fertilizers' letters, dated 18.02.2025 and 
05.06.2025. Revival decisions are continge nt to urea supply demand 
dynamics in the country; however, the recommendations of the Committee 
have been noted. Towards this direction, a VC meeting was held on 
04.09.2025 between CMD HFCL -cum-Addl. Secretary, Department of 
Fertilizers and CEO, ADDA confi rming payment position on part of HFCL with 
the request to execute the lease deed in favour of HFCL in Durgapur. This 
has been followed by a request, dated 04.11.2025 to the State Government 
of West Bengal for early finalization of the matter. ” 
    
OBSERVATION/RECOMMENDATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
1.7 The Committee note that the Department’s reply effectively defers a 
decision on the revival of the Durgapur and Haldia units of HFCL and the 
Korba unit of FCIL to a future stage, based on the demand supply gap of urea 
after the operationalization of existing plants. No concrete timeline, techno 
economic feasibility study, or policy framework has been provided for these 
idle units. While the Committee note that a video conference meeting was 
held on 04.09.2025 regarding the Durgapur lease deed and that a request 
was made to the Government of West Bengal on 04.11.2025, these remain 

 4 
 
preliminary administrative steps and fall short of the timely and effective 
policy initiatives envisaged by the Committee.  The Committee note that 
domestic urea production stood at 307 LMT against consumption of 388 LMT 
in 2024–25, with demand projected to rise to 444 LMT by 2035 –36. In this 
context, the Committee are of the view that existing idle infrastructure may 
merit closer consideration in the overall strategy for enhancing domestic 
capacity. The Korba unit of FCIL, despite its locational advantage i n 
Chhattisgarh, has not been specifically addressed in the Government’s 
reply. The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Government may 
consider examining the feasibility of revival of the Durgapur, Haldia and 
Korba units in a time bound manner, in alignment with evolving demand 
supply dynamics. The Department may also consider commissioning techno 
economic feasibility studies for these units, including assessment of 
appropriate technological options such as coal gasification for Korba, and 
appraise the Committee of the outcomes. The Committee would also 
appreciate being kept informed of the progress regarding finalization of the 
Durgapur lease deed with the Government of West Bengal. 
RECOMMENDATION SL. No. 5 
  
Production Continuity Clause for Sale/Disinvestment of Fertilizer Units 
1.8   Noting the decline in domestic urea production and the adverse impact of 
sale of a private fertilizer plant on national production capacity , the Committee 
recommended as under: - 
 
      “The Committee note that the production of Urea during 2023-24 was 314 
LMT and it has come down to 307 LMT during the year 2024-25.  
The Committee were further note that the decrease in production capacity was 
because one private plant with an annual capacity of 12 LMT has been sold and 
is out of Urea.  As the Country is dependent on imports in the sector, the 
Committee are of the opini on that the Government may formulate its policies to 
regulate the sale/ disinvestment process of fertilizer units, etc. so as to mandate 
production continuity clause(s) which may require the purchaser(s) to continue 
with the production of Urea/ other fertilizer, so that the production capacity of the 
Country remains maintained and the import burden gets reduced. The Committee 
may be apprised of the action taken in this matter.” 
 

 5 
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERMENT   
1.9  In their action taken reply to the afore -mentioned recommendation of the 
Committee, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Department of Fertilizers 
has stated as under: - 
“With regard to Urea, the Government had announced New Investment 
Policy (NIP) – 2012 on 2nd January, 2013 and its amendment on 7th October, 
2014 to facilitate fresh investment in the Urea sector and to make India self -
sufficient in the Urea sector. Total 6 new Urea units have been set up under NIP-
2012 which includes 4 Urea units set up through Joint Venture Companies (JVC) 
of nominated PSUs and 2 Urea units set up by the private companies. The units 
set up through JVC are Ramagundam Urea unit of Ramagundam Fertilizers and 
Chemicals Ltd (RFCL) in Telangana and 3 Urea units name ly Gorakhpur, Sindri 
and Barauni of Hindustan Urvarak & Rasayan Limited (HURL) in Uttar Pradesh, 
Jharkhand and Bihar, respectively. The units set up by private companies are 
Panagarh Urea unit of Matix Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd. (Matix) in West 
Bengal; and Gadepan-III Urea unit of Chambal Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd. 
(CFCL) in Rajasthan. Each of these units has installed capacity of 12.7 Lakh 
Metric Tonne per annum (LMTPA). These units are highly energy efficient as they 
are based on latest technology. Therefore, these units have together added Urea 
production capacity of 76.2 LMTPA, thereby total indigenous Urea production 
capacity (Reassessed Capacity, RAC) has increased from 207.54 LMTPA during 
2014-15 to 283.74 LMTPA during 2023 -24. Further, an exc lusive policy for the 
revival of Talcher unit of FCIL through JVC of nominated PSUs namely Talcher 
Fertilizers Limited (TFL) by setting up a new Greenfield Urea plant of 12.7 LMTPA 
at coal gasification route has also been approved. Recently, the Union Cabi net 
has approved the proposal for setting up of a new Brownfield Ammonia -Urea 
Complex of 12.7 Lakh Metric Tonnes (LMT) annual capacity of Urea production 
within the existing premises of Brahmaputra Valley Fertilizer Corporation Limited 
(BVFCL), Namrup, Assam which will be named as Assam Valley Fertilizer and 
Chemical Company Ltd. (AVFCCL). These two projects are under execution 
phase. 
In addition, the Government also notified the New Urea Policy (NUP) – 
2015 on 25th May, 2015 for the existing 25 gas-based Urea units with one of the 
objectives of maximizing indigenous Urea production beyond RAC.  The NUP -
2015 has led to additional production of Urea by 20-25 LMT as compared to the 
production during 2014-15 annually. 
Above steps together have facilitated increase of Urea production from 
level of 225 LMT per annum during 2014-15 to 306.67 LMT of Urea during 2024-
25.” 
 

 6 
 
 OBSERVATION/RECOMMENDATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
1.10  The Committee note with concern that the Government’s reply does 
not adequately address the specific issue raised, namely the need for a 
policy provision mandating production continuity clauses in the event of 
sale or disinvestment of fertilizer units. The Committee had highlighted the 
case of a private plant with an annual capacity of 12 LMT which ceased urea 
production following its sale, contributing to a decline in national 
production from 314 LMT in 2023 24 to 307 LMT in 2024 25. However, the 
reply reiterates general information regarding NIP 2012 and capacity 
additions under the joint ventur e route, without addressing the regulatory 
gap identified. The Committee observe that there appears to be no clearly 
defined mechanism at present to ensure continuity of urea or other fertilizer 
production after the transfer or sale of such units. The reply has neither 
clarified this position nor indicated any specific remedial framework. In this 
context, the Committee recommend that the Government may consider 
examining the feasibility of introducing appropriate policy provisions to 
ensure production continuity in cases of sale, disinvestment, or change of 
use of fertilizer manufacturing units. This may include suitable 
modifications to existing policy frameworks such as NIP 2012, the Fertilizer 
Control Order, or other relevant instruments. 
 
RECOMMENDATION SL. No. 9 
  
Development of Indigenous Technology for Fertilizer Manufacturing:  
1.11   Highlighting India’s continued dependence on foreign licensors for 
fertilizer plant technology despite strong domestic technical capacity , the 
Committee recommended as under: - 
 
      “The Committee find that despite having an excellent pool of engineers 
and managers in Urea plants, the Country still depend upon foreign companies 
for the basic license of running, repairing and making the plant with everything 
kept in the hands of the lic ensor. Admittedly, the indigenous ‘Chemical Process 
Technology Development for fertilizers’ encompasses various stages, from initial 
laboratory research to pilot testing to scale up and finally full -scale plant 
operation, often involving iterative c ycles of refinement entailing involvement of  
a massive investment in R&D in the field of synchronized pipe-based technology 

 7 
 
based on advance metallurgy, design and fabrication of all connected to overall 
objective to achieve better energy efficiency to minimize production costs. This 
integrated approach requires multiple institutional participation as Individual 
Companies on th eir own may not be suitable to develop end -to-end solution 
having competitive advantage and energy savings. Keeping in view the present 
constraints, the Committee feels the need to develop a self-sufficient indigenous 
eco system with integration of institu tions to develop a process technology for 
urea and complex fertilizers. The Committee were apprised by the Department’s 
representative during oral evidence that there were four Companies from the 
Netherlands, the USA, Italy and Japan which have authority t o grant the license 
in India. The Committee, therefore, feel the urgent need for development of 
indigenous technology for setting up fertilizer plants and maintaining them, 
through an integrated approach by engaging the best of institutions and technical 
experts in the field, backed by suitable Budgetary support and Government 
patronage, which will remove the technical constraints and dependence and 
speed up self -reliance in the sector. The Committee recommend that a special 
high power task force be constituted for this purpose at the earliest.” 
REPLY OF THE GOVERMENT   
1.12  In their action taken reply to the afore-mentioned recommendation of the 
Committee, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Department of Fertilizers 
has stated as under: - 
“Under NIP-2012, total 6 new Urea units have been set up which includes 4 Urea 
units set up through Joint Venture Companies (JVC) of nominated PSUs and 2 
Urea units set up by the private companies. The units set up through JVC are 
Ramagundam Urea unit of Ra magundam Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd (RFCL) 
in Telangana and 3 Urea units namely Gorakhpur, Sindri and Barauni of 
Hindustan Urvarak & Rasayan Limited (HURL) in Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and 
Bihar, respectively. The units set up by private companies are P anagarh Urea 
unit of Matix Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd. (Matix) in West Bengal; and Gadepan-
III Urea unit of Chambal Fertilizers and Chemicals Ltd. (CFCL) in Rajasthan. 
Each of these units has installed capacity of 12.7 Lakh Metric Tonne per annum 
(LMTPA). These units are highly energy efficient as they are based on latest 
technology. Therefore, these units have together added Urea production capacity 
of 76.2 LMTPA, thereby total indigenous Urea production capacity (Reassessed 
Capacity, RAC) has increased  from 207.54 LMTPA during 2014 -15 to 283.74 
LMTPA during 2023-24.” 
 OBSERVATION/RECOMMENDATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
1.13  The Committee note that the Government’s reply does not address 
the specific recommendation regarding the constitution of a High Power 

 8 
 
Task Force for the development of indigenous process technology for urea 
and complex fertilizers. The response is confined to capacity additions 
under NIP 2012 and does not engage with the issue of technological 
indigenization highlighted by the Committee.  The Committee had drawn 
attention to India’s continued reliance on a limited number of foreign 
licensors for core technology in urea plant design and operations. This 
dependence has implications for long term self-reliance and technological 
capability in the fertilizer sector. In this context, the Committee are of the 
view that capacity augmentation, while important, may be complemented 
by parallel efforts towards strengthening indigenous technological 
capabilities. The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Government 
may consider examining the feasibility of constituting an appropriate 
institutional mechanism, such as a High -Power Task Force, with 
participation from the Department of Fertilizers, leading scientifi c and 
research institutions, and industr y stakeholders, to explore the 
development of indigenous process technologies for urea and complex 
fertilizers. Such a mechanism may also outline a phased research and 
development roadmap, identify resource requirements, and facilitate 
coordinated efforts across institutions. The Committee would appreciate 
being apprised of the steps taken in this regard, along with a more focused 
response on the issue of technological indigenization. 
 
RECOMMENDATION SL. No. 25 
 
Central Monitoring Mechanism Against Fertilizer Shortage and Black -
Marketing:  
1.14   Expressing concern over fertilizer shortages and instances of black-
marketing arising from shortfall in imports and international supply disruptions,  
the Committee recommended as under: - 
 
      “The Committee note that only 19.7 LMT of P&K fertilizers were imported 
during the year against the targeted import of 30 LMT by the companies under 
Open General License, due to their financial compulsions. This resulted in the 
shortage of DAP in the Countr y and led to its black marketing.  Moreover, there 
was shortage of fertilizers especially, DAP in the Country, due to international 

 9 
 
factors, as a particular Country did not supply fertilizers to India. Keeping in view 
that the matter is of serious concern, the Committee desire that a Central 
monitoring mechanism be developed to take timely effective actions during such 
emergent situati ons and a policy be framed for suitable action against the 
defaulting agencies, etc.” 
REPLY OF THE GOVERMENT   
1.15  In their action taken reply to the afore -mentioned recommendation of the 
Committee, the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Department of Fertilizers 
has stated as under: - 
“In case of Phosphatic and Potassic (P&K) fertilizers, Government has 
implemented Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) Policy w.e.f. 01.04.2010. Under the 
policy, a fixed amount of subsidy, decided on annual/bi-annual basis, is provided 
to manufacturer / importer on notified P&K fertilizers depending on their nutrient 
content i.e. N itrogen (N), Phosphorus (P), Potassium (K) and Sulphur (S) to 
improve availability of fertilizers to farmers. In view of price volatility in 
international prices of key fertilizers and raw materials, the Government 
subsumes fluctuations, if any, while fixi ng NBS rates for P&K fertilizers 
annually/bi-annually Under the NBS policy, P&K fertilizers are covered under 
Open General License (OGL) and companies are free to import /produce these 
fertilizers as per their business dynamics. However, the suggestion of the 
committee has been noted for necessary compliance.” 
 OBSERVATION/RECOMMENDATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
1.16  The Committee note that the reply furnished by the Government does 
not adequately address the specific recommendations made. The response 
largely reiterates the provisions of the NBS policy framework and the OGL 
regime, which are already on record, and does not engage with the issues 
raised by the Committee regarding the need for a central monitoring 
mechanism during emergent shortage situat ions and a policy framework 
to address instances of non fulfilment of import commitments. The 
observation that the suggestion of the Committee has been noted does not 
provide clarity on the action proposed to be taken.  The Committee note 
with concern that the shortfall of nearly 10.3 LMT against the targeted 
import of 30 LMT of P and K fertilizers contributed to supply constraints, 
adversely affecting availability during the cropping season. The existing 
framework, wherein OGL importers operate based on com mercial 
considerations, may benefit from suitable safeguards to ensure timely and 

 10 
 
adequate availability in critical periods.  In this context, the Committee 
recommend that the Government may consider strengthening the existing 
framework by examining the feasibility of instituting a suitable monitoring 
arrangement to track import trends and anticipate potential shortages. The 
Committee also suggest that appropriate policy options may be explored 
to address situations where import commitments are not met, and to 
ensure timely corrective measures. Further, the possibility of developing 
contingency arrangements, including alternative sourcing mechanisms 
through public sector entities or other channels, may also be examined to 
mitigate supply disruptions.  The Committee would appreciate being 
apprised of the steps taken in this regard. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 11 
 
 
CHAPTER II 
OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT 
Recommendation Sl. No. 1 
Promotion of fertilizers production: Need for Enhancing Domestic 
Production Capacity (Urea, DAP, NPK, SSP) 
 
2.1 The Committee, in their Fifteenth Report (18th Lok Sabha), had recommended as 
under: – 
          “The Committee are happy to find record production of fertilizers during 
the FY 2024-25 viz production of P&K fertilizers (NPKS + DAP) increased from 
138 LMT in 2021 to 158.78 LMT in 2024 -25; SSP production increased from 
49.35 LMT to 52.44 LMT; with a record total overall domestic production of 
fertilizers (Urea + P&K + SSP) increase d to 517.89 LMT which is statedly the 
highest ever. The Committee note that against the Urea consumption of 388 LMT 
during the year 2024-25 the indigenous production has been only 307 LMT. The 
consumption of Urea is projected to be 444 LMT during the year 2035-36. The 
Committee further find that while the consumption of P&K fertilizers is projected 
to increase from 246 LMT during 2024 -25 to 305 LMT during 2035 -36 . 
Admittedly, to meet the requirements, India currently imports a significant share 
of its fertilizers, particularly potash and phosphate-based fertilizers along with raw 
materials like Natural gas used in urea production, thereby, exposing the Country 
to global market shocks, geopolitical risks and currency fluctuations. The 
Committee, are of the v iew that achieving self -sufficiency through domestic 
production, diversified sourcing and indigenous R&D can only help reduce these 
vulnerabilities and enhance strategic autonomy, while stabilizing subsidies and 
ensure timely availability of fertilizers to  farmers during critical crop seasons. In 
view of the foregoing, the Committee are, therefore, of the considered view that 
the Government need to augment capabilities in this sector to increase 
indigenous production of fertilizers in the Country through pr omotion of R&D in 
fertilizer sector and also plugging the present deficiencies in this sector through 
a holistic review of all inter related sectors with a view to attain self -sufficiency. 
The Committee also desire that, keeping in view of the import depen dence of 
fertilizer raw materials, the Government must further diversify its sources of 
import so as to offset the geopolitical compulsions.”

fertilizers, Government may come u p with new Green field and brown field 
fertilizer projects to minimize import requirements so that requisite fertilizers may

of urea during 2023-24 i.e. 39.7 percent of requirement, while imported 106 LMT

facilitating establishment of long term agreements and joint venture projects with

raw materials so as to secure regular resource access and supply chain stability 
for timely su pply of requirements at most competitive rates and to avoid price 
volatility. The Committee are of the considered opinion that this will also facilitate 
the fertilizer units to operate at optimum capacity without supply hindrances and 
effectively reduce th e subsidy burden. The Committee may be apprised of the 
action taken in the matter.”

Nano DAP, when used as a seed treatment and foliar spray, can significantly 
reduce the requirement for conventional granular DAP. Due to ongoing research 
in the field, the Gove rnment of India has notified Nano Urea with varying 
specifications and nitrogen content during the last few years. In view of the 
numerous benefits and advantages of Nano fertilizers, the Committee, strongly 
recommend that the Government may encourage vigorous Research in the field 
to promote development of more such Nano fertilizers variants (Macro and Micro 
nutrient grades)  through coordinated approach involving both the Public and 
Private sector companies, in order to ensure self -sufficiency in fertilizers for 
sustainable agriculture.   The Committee further desire that the Department of 
Fertilizers may work-out and seek for allocation of sufficient funds for developing 
innovative nano fertilizers so that it gets focused attention and ensure regular 
supply of various fertilizers at reasonable rates, ease subsidy burden and help 
save precious foreign exchange by reducing the import burden of the Country.”

Recommendation No. 1 
 
1.5.   The Committee made the following recommendation regarding fixing periodic 
targets for development of Pesticide formulation: 
 
 The Committee note that IPFT was established way back in the year 1991 as an 
Autonomous Institute under the Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, Ministry 
of Chemicals and Fertilizers as the successor of Pesticide Development Program in India 
(PDPI), which was established in the year 1986 in collaboration with the Government of 
India by the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO). As regards 
achieving goals and objectives by IPFT, the Committee note that since the inception of 
IPFT, it has developed 86 pesticide formulations, out of which 64 technologies have been 
transferred to Industries. The Committee also note that IPFT has inter-alia developed 47 
new formulations besides engaging in other activities like conducting analytical studies, 
filing of Patents and Research Papers, etc. The Committee, however note with concern 
that IPFT had not fixed any periodic targets for development of pes ticide formulation, 
quantum of new formulations for transferring them to Industries in the last 34 years of its 
functioning. The Committee further note that during the huge time period of 34 years of 
its functioning which spans more than three (03) decades IPFT has developed 86 
pesticide formulations amounting to a meager 2.5 percent pesticides formul ations per 
year. The Committee observe with dissatisfaction, the slow pace of IPFT and desire that 
they may be apprised about the precise reasons for non -fixation of yearly targets. The 
Committee recommend that IPFT should immediately review its functionin g in 
consultation with the Department and bring forth initiatives for development of pesticide 
formulations at a faster pace as per the needs of the industries as well as farmer 
communities across the Country. 
 
1.6 In their Action Taken Note furnished to the Committee, the Department of 
Chemicals and Petrochemicals has stated as under: 
 
“The facts and figures as observed by the Hon’ble Committee are respectfully 
noted. However, it is submitted that IPFT has consistently aligned its activities with 
the evolving needs of the agrochemical industry and the agricultural sector. The 
Institute remains committed to  identifying and expanding areas for growth in the 
development and transfer of pesticide formulation technologies. 
It is pertinent to mention that pesticide formulation development is largely demand-
driven and market -oriented. IPFT undertakes development of formulation 
technologies based on specific requirements of the agrochemical industry, 
including molecule -specific and application -oriented needs. The Institute 

3 
 
possesses the requisite expertise and infrastructure to meet such demands of the 
industry. In this context, IPFT has developed 86 formulation technologies and 
successfully transferred 6 4 technologies to industry for commercialization , 
reflecting its sustained contribution to the agrochemical sector. 
The development of pesticide formulations is a complex, multi -stage process , 
involving laboratory research, bio -evaluation, pilot -scale optimization, and 
compliance with regulatory requirements prescribed by the Central Insecticides 
Board and Registration Committee (CIB&RC). These processes are inherently 
time-intensive and resou rce-driven, and therefore not amenable to rigid annual 
numerical targets. 
Further, formulation development constitutes only one of the core activities of 
IPFT. The Institute also undertakes: 
• Comprehensive chemical characterization and analytical studies 
• Residue monitoring and risk assessment , including long -term studies in districts 
of Haryana and collaborative work in Rajasthan 
• Support and promote the regulatory compliance and quality assurance 
In the last few decades, the issue of pesticide residues in food commodities and 
environment spheres has predominantly gained the attention of all stakeholders 
and IPFT has strategically shifted focus towards development of safer, residue -
minimized, and eco-friendly formulations, including biopesticides. The Institute is 
actively working towards establishing a biofoundry facility in collaboration with the 
Department of Biotechnology under the BioE3 policy, aiming to provide an 
integrated platform for development and evaluation of biopesticides derived from 
plant, microbial, and waste-based resources. 
IPFT has also undertaken extensive farmer outreach and capacity -building 
initiatives, conducting over 40 awareness programmes across more than 25 
districts in 10 states, promoting safe pesticide use, integrated pest management, 
and adoption of biopesticides for sustainable agriculture. It is further submitted that 
the scope of IPFT’s work could not be viable to be restricted to fixed formulation 
targets, as the requirements of the agrochemical sector are dynamic and 
influenced by regulatory, environmental, and market considerations . IPFT 
reiterates its commitment to enhancing its performance and contributing effectively 
to the needs of the agrochemical industry and farming community in a sustainable 
and impactful manner”. 
Comments of the Committee 
1.7 The Committee had observed that during the last 34 years, IPFT had 
developed only 86 formulations out of which only  64 technologies could be 
transferred to the industries.  The Committee had also pointed out that no yearly 
targets were fixed by IPFT.  In their Action Taken Notes, it had been submitted that 
development of pesticide formulations was a complex, multi -stage process, 
involving laboratory research, bio -evaluation, pilot -scale optimization and 

4 
 
compliance with regulatory requirements prescribed by the Central Insecticides 
Board and Registration Committee (CIB&RC). These processes were inherently 
time-intensive and resource -driven and therefore not amenable to rigid annual 
numerical targets. The Committee does not find  this contention totally acceptable 
and are of the considered view that some guiding principles be laid down for the 
functioning of the IPFT with quantifiable targets fixed not only for development of 
formulations but also for comprehensive chemical characterization and analytical 
studies, residue monitoring and risk assessment for long-term studies in Districts 
of Haryana and collaborative work in Rajasthan , the Committee are of the 
considered view that qualitative and quantitative targets may be fixed for 
promoting regulatory compliance and quality assurance for conducting of farmers 
awareness programmes across the Country. In the absence of concrete data, the 
Committee do not find convincing the contention of IPFT that it had consistently  
aligned its activities with the evolving needs of the agrochemical industry and the 
agricultural sector  and t he Institute remain ed committed to identifying and 
expanding areas for growth in the development and transfer of pesticide 
formulation technologies. The Committee reiterate that broad targets in respect of 
various aspect of functioning of the IPFT may be laid down and the Committee be 
apprised of the steps taken in this regard. 
Recommendation No. 3  
1.8 The Committee made the following recommendation regarding fixing reasonable 
prices for New Generation Pesticides: 
 
The Committee were informed that new generation pesticides formulation 
technologies, which are being developed by the IPFT are better than the conventional 
pesticides formulations containing large amount petroleum derived organic solvents and 
composed of f ine dusty powders. The Committee, however note that price of new 
generation pesticide formulations depends on the type of pesticides, formulation 
technology, concentration and brand and the actual market price was determined by the 
industry partner, taking  into account production cost, commercialization strategy and 
affordability for farmers. The Committee observe that the price fixation of new generation 
pesticide formulations, if left totally to the industry partner with IPFT having no say in this 
regard, may leave scope for manipulation by the industry partner. The Committee are of 
the considered view that the new generation pesticides formulation which are much better 

5 
 
than the conventional pesticides formulations must reach farmers all across the country 
so that the benefits of new generation pesticides formulation developed by IPFT are 
reaped proportionately by one and all across the agriculture sector. The Committee 
desire that the IPFT and the Department work together in tandem and recommend that 
appropriate steps be taken for determination of reasonable prices for new generation 
pesticides formulation of IPFT so as to make it available to the farmers at affordable 
prices. The Committee may be apprised of the action taken in this regard. 
 
1.9 In their Action Taken Note furnished to the Committee, the Department of 
Chemicals and Petrochemicals has stated as under: 
 
“The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted. It is submitted that IPFT has 
been actively engaged in the development of new generation pesticide formulation 
technologies, which are cost-effective, safer, environmentally benign, and superior 
to conventional solvent-based and dust formulations. 
 
It is respectfully submitted that price determination of pesticide formulations is 
governed by market dynamics, including cost of raw materials, scale of production, 
regulatory compliance, distribution channels, and commercial strategies of the 
industry pa rtner. As per the existing framework, IPFT transfers technologies to 
industry for commercialization, and the pricing is determined by the industry based 
on the manufacturing and marketing over-heads. 
However, IPFT recognizes the concern of the Hon’ble Committee regarding 
affordability and accessibility to farmers, and has taken/initiated the following 
steps: 
• Development of cost -effective and scalable formulations, including water -
based and solvent-free technologies, to reduce production costs. 
• Promotion of multiple licensing of technologies to avoid monopolistic 
practices and enhance competitive pricing. 
• Focus on biopesticides and green formulations, which are inherently safer 
and can be produced at decentralized levels. 
• Engagement with farmer producer organizations (FPOs), cooperatives, and 
public sector agencies for wider outreach”. 
 
 
Comments of the Committee 
 
1.10 Noting the benefits of new generation pesticides formulation technologies , 
the Committee  had emphasized that these formulation must reach all farmers 
across the Country so that benefits are reaped across the agriculture sector.  
However, the Department in its Action Taken notes  has submitted that price 
determination of pesticide formulations was governed by market dynamics, 
including cost of raw materials, scale of production, regulatory compliance, 
distribution channels and commercial strategies of the industry partner. As per the 
existing framework, IPFT transfers technologies to industry for commercialization 

6 
 
and pricing is determined by the industry based on the manufacturing and 
marketing over-heads. The Committee are of the considered view that IPFT need 
to take some proactive steps to make the new generation pesticides formulation 
technologies across the agriculture sector. The Committee, therefore, reiterate its 
earlier recommendation that the Department as well as IPFT must design a way out 
to ensure that benefits of new generation pesticides formulation technologies 
reaches across the Country and to each and every farmer invariably as IPFT is 
stated to be engaged in public welfare-oriented research.  The Committee would 
like to be apprised of the steps taken by the Department in this regard. 
 
Recommendation No. 6  
 
1.11 The Committee made the following recommendation regarding further 
strengthening the function of IPFT: 
 
 As regards new generation pesticides formulation for agriculture and as well as for 
household pest management and their pricing, the Committee were informed that IPFT 
was a Research and Development Institute focused on the development of pesticides 
formulation technologies and it does not engage in production or marketing of any of its 
formulations. The IPFT after development of formulations merely transfers the 
technologies to the industries for commercial production and marketing. The Committee 
are intrigued about the reasons restricting the IPFT for production and marketing of its 
formulations despite being in existence for 34 years. The Committee therefore, desired 
that IPFT come up with feasibility studies towards expanding its ventures for production 
as well as market its formulations in the coming future. The Committee note that as 
regards the size of IPFT, it is very small as compared to its objectives and mandate. IPFT 
has however submitted that based on the emerging needs of the sector, the capacity  of 
IPFT can be strengthened. The Committee are of the considered view that it is high time 
for the IPFT to go for deep introspection for further strengthening its functions including 
mass production and marketing of its own products so that the institute can successfully 
compete with the private players in the market. The Committee would like to be apprised 
of the steps taken in this regard.  
 
 
1.12 In their Action Taken Note furnished to the Committee, the Department of

4.1   The Committee made the following recommendation regarding fixing periodic targets 
for development of Pesticide formulation:

Autonomous Institute under the Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, Ministry 
of Chemicals and Fertilizers as the successor of Pesticide Development Program in India 
(PDPI), which was established in the year 1986 in collaboration with the Government of 
India by the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO). As regards 
achieving goals and objectives by IPFT, the Committee note that since the inception of 
IPFT, it has developed 86 pesticide formulations, out of which 64 technologies have been 
transferred to Industries. The Committee also note that IPFT has inter-alia developed 47

filing of Patents and Research Papers, etc. The Committee, however note with concern 
that IPFT had not fixed any periodic targets for development of pes ticide formulation, 
quantum of new formulations for transferring them to Industries in the last 34 years of its 
functioning. The Committee further note that during the huge time period of 34 years of 
its functioning which spans more than three (03) decades  IPFT has developed 86 
pesticide formulations amounting to a meager 2.5 percent pesticides formulations per 
year. The Committee observe with dissatisfaction, the slow pace of IPFT and desire that 
they may be apprised about the precise reasons for non -fixation of yearly targets. The 
Committee recommend that IPFT should immediately review its functioning in 
consultation with the Department and bring forth initiatives for development of pesticide 
formulations at a faster pace as per the needs of the industries  as well as farmer 
communities across the Country.

“The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted. It is submitted that IPFT has 
been actively engaged in the development of new generation pesticide formulation 
technologies, which are cost-effective, safer, environmentally benign, and superior 
to conventional solvent-based and dust formulations. 
 
It is respectfully submitted that price determination of pesticide formulations is 
governed by market dynamics, including cost of raw materials, scale of production, 
regulatory compliance, distribution channels, and commercial strategies of the 
industry pa rtner. As per the existing framework, IPFT transfers technologies to 
industry for commercialization, and the pricing is determined by the industry based 
on the manufacturing and marketing over-heads. 
However, IPFT recognizes the concern of the Hon’ble Committee regarding 
affordability and accessibility to farmers, and has taken/initiated the following 
steps: 
• Development of cost -effective and scalable formulations, including water -
based and solvent-free technologies, to reduce production costs. 
• Promotion of multiple licensing of technologies to avoid monopolistic 
practices and enhance competitive pricing. 
• Focus on biopesticides and green formulations, which are inherently safer 
and can be produced at decentralized levels. 
• Engagement with farmer producer organizations (FPOs), cooperatives, and 
public sector agencies for wider outreach”. 
 

23 
 
 
(Please see Para No. 1.10 of Chapter – I of the Report) 
Recommendation No. 6  
Competing in Market/Expansion of ventures 
4.5 The Committee made the following recommendation regarding further 
strengthening the function of IPFT: 
 
 As regards new generation pesticides formulation for agriculture and as well as for 
household pest management and their pricing, the Committee were informed that IPFT 
was a Research and Development Institute focused on the development of pesticides 
formulation technologies and it does not engage in production or marketing of any of its 
formulations. The IPFT after development of formulations merely transfers the 
technologies to the industries for commercial production and marketing. The Committee 
are intrigued about the reasons restricting the IPFT for production and marketing of its 
formulations despite being in existence for 34 years. The Committee therefore, desired 
that IPFT come up with feasibility studies towards expanding its ventures for production 
as well as market its formulations in the coming future. The Committee note that as 
regards the size of IPFT, it is very small as compared to its objectives and mandate. IPFT 
has however submitted that based on the emerging needs of the sector, the capacit y of 
IPFT can be strengthened. The Committee are of the considered view that it is high time 
for the IPFT to go for deep introspection for further strengthening its functions including 
mass production and marketing of its own products so that the institute can successfully 
compete with the private players in the market. The Committee would like to be apprised 
of the steps taken in this regard.  
 
4.6 In their Action Taken Note furnished to the Committee, the Department of 
Chemicals and Petrochemicals has stated as under: 
“The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted. It is respectfully submitted 
that IPFT was established as a specialized R&D institution with a mandate to 
develop, validate, and transfer pesticide formulation technologies to industry, 
rather than to unde rtake commercial production and marketing. This model has 
enabled IPFT to promote technology dissemination across multiple industry 
partners, avoid duplication of infrastructure, and support the broader agrochemical 
ecosystem. 
It is further submitted that production and marketing of pesticide formulations 
require significant investments in manufacturing infrastructure, regulatory 
approvals, distribution networks, and working capital, which are typically beyond 
the scope of a res earch-oriented institution. Accordingly, technology transfer to 
industry has been adopted as a scalable and efficient mechanism for 
commercialization. 
It is also submitted that IPFT’s current approach of non -exclusive technology 
transfer ensures wider availability of technologies, promotes competition, and 
prevents monopolistic practices in the market”. 
 

24 
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
(Please see Para No. 1.13 of Chapter – I of the Report) 
Recommendation No. 7  
Participation of Farmers in Awareness Programmes 
 
4.7 The Committee made the following recommendation regarding farmers awareness 
programmes: 
 
 
The Committee are happy to note that for promoting the safe use of pesticides, 
IPFT had initiated farmer awareness programmes. These programmes were stately 
initiated in the year 2022-2023. The Committee further note that from the year 2022-2023 
to 2024-2025, a total of 32 such programmes were conducted by IPFT where a total of 
just 9223 farmers participated in these programmes who provided positive feedback.  The 
Committee find these figures grossly inadequate keeping in view the fact that the farmers 
across the Country totals to more than 10 crores. The Committee, therefore, recommend 
that the IPFT and the Department come out with a roadmap to conduct such programmes 
periodically and to encourage more and more farmers to participate in them so that the 
benefits are reaped by all farmers across the nation.  
 
4.8 In their Action Taken Note furnished to the Committee, the Department of 
Chemicals and Petrochemicals has stated as under: 
 “The Department through IPFT has been organizing farmer awareness 
programmes across the country to enhance farmers’ knowledge regarding the use 
of new -generation pesticide formulations in agricultural practices. These 
programmes are aimed at educating farmers on the safe, judicious, and effective 
use of pesticides, parti cularly highlighting the advantages of new -generation 
formulations that offer improved efficacy, lower dosage requirements, and 
comparatively reduced environmental impact. Farmers are also sensitized about 
safe handling practices, proper application techni ques, and the importance of 
adhering to the guidelines issued by the Central Insecticides Board and 
Registration Committee. During the last four years, from 2022 –23 to 2024-25, 32 
farmer awareness programmes  have been organized by IPFT in remote areas 
across various States of the country. During the year 2025 -26, 11 such farmers 
awareness programs were organized in 6 different states and 4565 farmers had 
participated. In total, these 43 programmes during the period 2022-23 to 2025-26 
have benefited more tha n 15,000 farmers, who received training and awareness 
in local languages”.  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
(Please see Para No. 1.16 of Chapter – I of the Report) 
 
Recommendation No. 9 
Optimum Utilization of IPFT infrastructure 
4.9 The Committee made the following recommendation regarding optimum utilization 
of IPFT infrastructure: 
 
 The Committee note that IPFT at present has laboratories under its three divisions 

25 
 
viz (i) Formulation division, (ii) Analytical division and (iii) Bio -Science division. The 
formulation division is stated to have laboratory set up for development of pesticides 
formulations for agricultural as well as household pest management and it also have pilot 
plant facility that can scale up lab scale research to a commerci al production with 
optimum budget and it has capacity to produce upto 100 kg. per shift. Similarly the 
analytical division is accredited and equipped with chemical testing of pesticides. The 
bio-science division is equipped to evaluate the different pestic ides formulations by the 
IPFT or by the industry for their commercial viability through well -equipped bio -assay 
laboratory, green house/ glass house and experimental field trials. Admittedly, IPFT has 
pilot plant facilities but was never utilized for comme rcial production. The Committee 
deplore the same and recommend that the IPFT should initiate ameliorative steps for full 
capacity utilization of its installed capacities in so far as plants and laboratories are 
concerned. To this extant, the Committee desire that appropriate monitoring mechanism 
be put in place to ensure optimum capacity utilisation of IPFT infrastructure. 
 
4.10 In their Action Taken Note furnished to the Committee, the Department of 
Chemicals and Petrochemicals has stated as under: 
“The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted. It is submitted that IPFT has 
established well-equipped infrastructure comprising Formulation, Analytical, and 
Bio-Science divisions, including pilot plant facilities for scale -up of laboratory -
developed technologies. 
It is respectfully submitted that the pilot plant facility is primarily intended for 
process optimization, validation, and demonstration of technologies prior to 
transfer to industry, rather than for continuous commercial production. This 
approach ensures that technologies are developed, standardized, and transferred 
efficiently to industry for large-scale manufacturing. 
However, the concern of the Hon’ble Committee regarding optimal utilization of 
infrastructure is duly acknowledged. In this regard, IPFT has identified the 
following steps: 
• Strengthening inter-division integration (Formulation, Analytical, Bio-
Science) for end-to-end utilization of facilities; 
• Establishment of a centralized monitoring mechanism for tracking 
infrastructure utilization, including: 
• Periodic review of facility usage; 
• Performance indicators for each division”.

Recommendation No. 11 
Analyzing the reasons for non-transfer of 22 formulations. 
 
 
4.11  The Committee made the following recommendation regarding non transference 

26 
 
of remaining 22 formulations to the industries: 
 
 
The Committee note that since inception of the IPFT, it has developed 86 
pesticides formulations out of which, only 64 technologies have been transferred. A total 
of 22 pesticides formulations could not be transferred according to IPFT. Stately, the 
market for bio-based formulations was not very robust at present and even if IPFT was

farmers. The Committee would like to be apprised of the steps taken in this regard.  
 
4.12 In their Action Taken Note furnished to the Committee, the Department of 
Chemicals and Petrochemicals has stated as under: 
“The observation of the Hon’ble Committee is noted. It is submitted that out of 86 
pesticide formulation technologies developed by IPFT, 64 technologies have been 
successfully transferred to industry, while 22 technologies could not be transferred 
due to a combination of technical, market, and regulatory factors. 
It is further submitted that the majority of the 22 non -transferred technologies 
pertain to bio-based pesticide formulations and nano-formulations. 
In respect of bio-based formulations, these have largely been developed under 
externally funded R&D projects (e.g., NASF) and are currently at different stages 
of development. The processes of comprehensive evaluation, field trials, and 
subsequent pilot -scale optimization  are underway, which are prerequisites for 
regulatory approval and technology transfer. These technologies are expected to 
be taken up for commercialization upon successful completion of these stages. 
In respect of nano-formulations, these have been developed as part of advanced 
research initiatives at IPFT . However, at present, there is no specific regulatory 
framework or approval mechanism available under the Central Insecticides Board 
and Registration Committee (CIB&RC) for such formulations. This regulatory gap 
is a key constraint in transferring these technologies to industry for commercial 
production. IPFT is actively engaging with stakeholders and monitoring 
developments in the regulatory domain, and will facilitate technology transfer as 
and when appropriate regulatory guidelines are established”.

Observation/Recommendation No. 1 
 
NEED FOR REVIEW IN THE PRICE REGULATION FRAMEWORK OF MEDICINES 
 
1.5.   The Committee made the following recommendation regarding undertaking a 
comprehensive review of the extant price regulation framework: 
 
“The Committee note that a wide range of frequently prescribed medicines, used for 
common ailments and chronic conditions are being sold at a high prices with unjustified 
trade margin. When asked about the huge differential in price to supplier viz-a-viz MRPs of 
the medicines, the Department has cited reasons such as distribution cost, etc which was 
not found convincing. When asked about the Departments inaction to curb the trade margins 
to the tune of 600% to 1100% in common medications, the Department’s reply appears 
unsatisfactory as it relied heavily on a general explanation of the Drugs (Prices Control) 
Order, 2013 (DPCO, 2013). The apparent lack of any control over trade margins, especially 
in the case of non-scheduled drugs, leaves the door open for widespread profiteering at the 
cost of patients.  The Committee desire that the Department undertake a comprehensive 
review of the extant price regulation framework to plug the existing loopholes in the pricing 
mechanism effecting the ordinary citizen.” 
 
 
1.6    In their Action Taken Notes, the Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers (Department of 
Pharmaceuticals) submitted as under: 
 
“The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Policy (NPPP), 2012, provides the regulatory 
framework for price of drugs and is given effect through the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 
2013 (DPCO, 2013).  The key principles of regulation of pricing of drugs under NPPP, 2012 
are essentiality of drugs, market-based pricing and control of formulation prices only.  Based 
on the provisions of DPCO 2013, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) 
fixes the ceiling prices of scheduled formulations listed in Schedule -I of the DPCO, 2013; 
retail price of new drugs as defined under para 2(1)(u) of the DPCO, 2013 and monitors the 
increase in the maximum retail price (MRP) of non-scheduled drugs which are not permitted 
to increase their MRP by more than 10% of their MRP during the preceding twelve months. 
 
As per Pharmarack database for financial year 2024-2025, which covers about 98000 SKUs, 
the market share of the scheduled formulations is approximately 18% of the total value and 
the market share of the non -scheduled formulations is approximately 82% of to tal value. 
Further, analysis of Pharmarack database shows that majority (approximately 87%) of the 
non-scheduled market is availing weighted average markup (margin for distributor & retailer 
as a percentage of price to distributor) up to 45%. Out of total non-scheduled market, 
approximately 4% are having the weighted average markup more than 100% of the price to 
distributor. Thus, the high margin is not the industry norm but is observed only in case of 

3 
 
small fraction of the market.   NPPA has taken steps, from time -to-time, to rationalise high 
trade margin which are as follows: 
 
(i) The MRP of 106 non -scheduled drug formulations were capped in 2014, which includes 
22 diabetic and 84 cardiovascular drugs. 
(ii) A cap on Trade Margin @ 30% on 42 selected non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines was 
put under ‘Trade Margin Rationalisation’ approach  in February, 2019. Under this, price of 
526 brands of medicines were reduced by an average of around 50% leading to annual 
savings of ₹984 crore to the patients. 
(iii) During COVID-19, the price of Oxygen Concentrators, Pulse Oximeter, Blood Pressure 
Monitoring Machine, Nebulizer, Digital Thermometer and Glucometer were regulated under 
“Trade Margin Rationalisation” approach by fixing trade margins on these devices in 
June/July 2021 under paragraph 19 of DPCO, 2013. 
 
Trade margin rationalisation (TMR) approach for regulating prices is undertaken under 
paragraph 19 of DPCO, 2013 which provides for fixation of prices under extraordinary 
circumstances in public interest for a limited period. The Department has held extens ive 
consultations with all stakeholders on various issues concerning the existing pricing 
framework including, inter alia, incorporation of a suitable enabling provision in DPCO, 2013 
for a TMR approach.” 
 
 
  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
 
1.7 Noting that a wide range of frequently prescribed medicines used for common 
ailments and chronic conditions are being sold at high prices with unjustified trade margin, 
the Committee in their Fourteenth Report had desired that the Department undertake a 
comprehensive review of the extant price regulation framework to plug the existing 
loopholes in the pricing mechanism effecting the ordinary citizen. The Department in its 
Action Taken Reply has submitted that as per Pharmarack database for financial year 2024-
2025, which covers about 98000 Store Keeping Units ( SKUs), the market share of the 
scheduled formulations is approximately 18% of the total value and the market share of the 
non-scheduled formulations is approximately 82% of total value. The reply seems to be 
inadequate and not does not address the concerns of the Committee  regarding apparent 
lack of any control over trade margins, especially in the case of non-scheduled drugs, which 
leaves the door open for widespread profiteering at the cost of patient s. The Committee 
note with concern that a significant portion of the pharmaceutical market, approximately 
82%, comprises non -scheduled drugs and thus, around 70,000 SKUs  remain outside the 
ambit of direct price control. The Committee therefore reiterate their earlier 
recommendation and desire that existing mechanism of monitoring only annual MRP 
increase up to 10% in respect of non-scheduled drugs be revisited to mitigate any adverse 

4 
 
impact on patients, particularly in respect of chronic -care and life -saving medicines. The 
Committee also desire to be apprised regarding the details of the non-scheduled drugs, 
which as admitted by the Department, are having the weighted average markup more than 
100% of the price to distributor.  
 
Observation/Recommendation No. 2 
 
REGULATORY BLIND SPOTS IN DPCO, 2013: THE URGENT NEED TO EMPOWER NPPA 
  
1.8 The Committee made the following recommendation regarding curbing pricing malpractices 
in India’s pharmaceutical sector: 
 
“The Committee note that the existing Drugs (Prices Control) Order 2013 (DPCO) is 
structurally inadequate to curb pricing malpractices in India’s pharmaceutical sector. 
Whereas the DPCO empowers the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) to fix 
ceiling prices for drugs listed under the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), but it 
fails to extend this regulatory authority to the unscheduled drugs. As such the NPPA is not 
empowered to regulate trade margins for non NLEM drugs in cases where excessive 
markups are evident on widely used and lifesaving medicines. This regulatory gap allows 
manufacturers to launch non-scheduled formulations, both branded and generic, at arbitrary 
points. Although they are technically restricted from increasing the maximum retail price 
(MRP) by more than 10 percent annually, the absence of initial price fixation renders this 
control largely meaningless.  This loophole requires to be corrected. The  Price to Stockist 
(PTS) data also remains undisclosed to the public, as platforms like Pharma Sahi Daam and 
Sugam App shows only MRPs and failed to reveal the true extent of profiteering. Fixed dose 
combination (FDC) drugs, which account for a substantial  share of prescriptions in India, 
also remain outside the ambit of price regulation despite their widespread use and potential 
for irrational combinations.  The Committee therefore, recommend that the Department 
should look into the matter and initiate ame liorative steps in this regard.  The Committee 
would like to be apprised by the steps taken by the department.” 
 
1.9 In their Action Taken Notes, the Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers (Department of 
Pharmaceuticals) submitted as under: 
 
“The National Pharmaceuticals Pricing Policy, 2012 (NPPP, 2012), envisages putting in 
place a regulatory framework for the pricing of drugs that would not only ensure availability 
of essential medicines at reasonable price but also provide suﬃcient opportun ity for 
innovation and competition, supporting industry growth; and meeting goals of employment 
and shared economic well-being for all.   The objective of ensuring availability of essential 
medicines at reasonable price is met by controlling the prices of  medicines specified in 
National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) released and revised by Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare from time to time. NLEM contains such medicine which satisfy the priority 
health needs of the country’s population and are req uired to be made available within the 
context of functioning health system at all times in adequate quantity to serve the general 
public.    
 
In addition, the existing policy and regulatory regime has also given impetus to the sustained 
growth of the sector while balancing it with the objective of facilitating availability and 
accessibility of drugs in the country at reasonable price.  This is s ubstantiated by the fact 
that India is third largest producer of drugs in volume terms; that the prices of both scheduled 

5 
 
and non-scheduled formulations in India are comparatively lower as indicated in a study by 
IQVIA, a leading global life sciences consulting firm, which compared the top-selling dosage 
forms (tablets, liquids, capsules and injections) of top -selling therapeutic categories (anti -
infective, anti -cancer, cardiovascular and hormonal drugs) in India with select other 
countries; and, that India is one of the few countries which is net exporter of medicines in 
the world indicating to cost competitiveness of the dru gs in India.  The relatively lower 
prevailing prices in India and the market competition affects the business decision regarding 
launch price of manufacturers of non -scheduled formulations, both branded and generic.   
Further, ceiling price of fixed dose c ombination (FDC) drugs, that are considered essential 
for priority health need and hence included in NLEM, is fixed as per the provision of DPCO, 
2013 while increase in prices of non -scheduled FDCs are regulated as per the extant 
provision of DPCO, 2013 in this regard. Accordingly, the prices of FDCs are not outside the 
ambit of DPCO, 2013. 
 
Also, analysis of Pharmarack database for financial year 2024 -2025, which covers about 
98000 SKUs, shows that majority (approximately 87%) of the non -scheduled market is 
availing weighted average markup (margin for distributor & retailer as a percentage of price 
to distributor) up to 45%. Out of total non -scheduled market, approximately 4% are having 
the weighted average markup more than 100% of the price to distributor.  Thus, the high 
margin is not the industry norm but is observed only in case of small fraction of the market.  
However, Government is seized of the matter regarding high trade margin in some cases in 
some of the drugs and have taken measures to address the same from time -to-time by 
regulating their prices under trade margin rationalisation (TMR) approach using the 
provision under paragraph 19 of DPCO, 2013. The Department has held extensive 
consultations with all stakeholders on various issues concerning the existing pricing 
framework including, inter alia, incorporation of a suitable enabling provision in DPCO, 2013 
for a TMR approach and the issue is presently under consideration of the Department.”  
 
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
 
1.10 The Committee, in their Original Report, had highlighted inadequacy of the current

The Committee, in their Original Report, has observed that Fixed dose combination

remained outside the ambit of price regulation despite their widespread use and potential

for irrational combinations.  The Committee note t he Department's clarification in this

Observation/Recommendation No. 2 
 
REGULATORY BLIND SPOTS IN DPCO, 2013: THE URGENT NEED TO EMPOWER NPPA 
4.3 The Committee, in their Fourteenth Report (18th Lok Sabha), had recommended as under: 
 
 
 “The Committee note that the existing Drugs (Prices Control) Order 2013 (DPCO) is 
structurally inadequate to curb pricing malpractices in India’s pharmaceutical sector. Whereas the 
DPCO empowers the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) to fix ceiling prices for 
drugs listed under the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), but it fails to extend this 
regulatory authority to the unscheduled drugs. As such the NPPA is not empowered to regulate 
trade margins for non NLEM drugs in cases where excessive markups are evident on widely used 
and lifesaving medicines. This regulatory gap allows manufacturers to launch n on-scheduled 
formulations, both branded and generic, at arbitrary points. Although they are technically restricted 
from increasing the maximum retail price (MRP) by more than 10 percent annually, the absence of 
initial price fixation renders this control largely meaningless.  This loophole requires to be corrected.

Sahi Daam and Sugam App shows only MRPs and failed to reveal the true extent of profiteering. 
Fixed dose combination (FDC) drugs, which account for a substantial share of prescriptions in 
India, also remain outside the ambit of price regulation despite their widespread use and potential 
for irrational combinations.  The Committee therefore, recommend that the Department should look 
into the matter and initiate ameliorative steps in this regard.  The Committee would like to be 
apprised by the steps taken by the department.”

more in use as has been done in th e case of scheduled formulations. Where prices are under 
check with more effective control. The Committee would like to be apprised of the steps taken by 
the Department as well as NPPA in this regard.” 
 
 
Observation/Recommendation No. 7 
 
PHARMACEUTICAL POLICY 
 
4.10 The Committee, in their Fourteenth Report (18th Lok Sabha), had recommended as under: 
 
 
 “As regard pharmaceutical policy under consideration of the Department, the Committee 
has been apprised that it has held stakeholder consultations regarding various provisions of DPCO, 
2013. Further, various stakeholder groups and associations were also invited to make 
presentations and submissions and give their recommendations in the course of interactive 
deliberations. Presently, the matter was statedly under examination in the Department, where the 
suggestions and recommendations from stakeholders were being scrutinised. The Committee are 
of view that immediate steps should be taken to come forth with a pharmaceutical policy where the 
thrust should be to provide both scheduled as well as non-scheduled formulations to the people at 
affordable prices.” 
 
4.11 In their Action Taken Notes, the Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers (Department of 
Pharmaceuticals) submitted as under: 
 
 “The National Pharmaceuticals Pricing Policy, 2012 (NPPP, 2012) strives to achieve a 
balance between affordability and availability of drugs on the one hand and promotion of growth of 
industry on the other. One of the key principles for regulation of prices of drugs under NPPP, 2012 
is the essentiality of the drug. The “Essentiality” criteria for drugs under the NPPP -2012 is met by 
considering the medicines specified in the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) as released 
and revised by Ministry of Health and Family Welfare from time to time. NLEM contains such 
medicine which satisfy the priority health needs of the country’s population and are required to be 
made available within the context of functioning health system at all times in adequate quan tity to 
serve the general public. The drugs under NLEM are included in the Scheduled -I of DPCO, 2013 

28 
 
and are referred to as scheduled drugs for which NPPA fixes the ceiling prices as per the provisions 
of DPCO, 2013. The drugs not included in the NLEM and hence the Schedule -I of DPCO, 2013 
are referred as non-scheduled drug. With a view to keep a check on overall drugs prices, the prices 
of non-scheduled drugs are monitored as per provisions of paragraph 20 of DPCO, 2013 which 
requires manufacturers of non -scheduled drug to not increase the maximum retail price by more 
than 10% per annum.   
The NPPP, 2012 also envisages putting in place a regulatory framework for the pricing of drugs 
that would provide suﬃcient opportunity for innovation and competition, supporting industry growth; 
and meeting goals of employment and shared economic well-being for all.  Increasing the span of 
price control may not be consistent with these objectives.  The NPPP , 2012 also recognises control 
over drug prices as only one element of an overall strategy for provision of affordable healthcare, 
with programmes of aff ordable healthcare to a majority of the population in the form of direct 
Government healthcare, insurance and a well spread -out, low-cost Janaushadhi pharmacy chain 
programme being other elements of the strategy. Thus, the policy approach has been to 
complement price control with affordable health programmes, with a view to simultaneously 
achieve multiplicity of policy objectives.  In this context, various measures taken by the Government 
to improve the access of medicines at reasonable rates to the common man are as follows:  
(vi) The Government has launched the Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana  
scheme with the objective of making quality generic medicines available at affordable prices 
to all. Under the scheme, dedicated outlets known as Jan Aushadhi Kendras (JAKs) have 
been opened to provide quality generic medicines at rates that are typically  50% to 80% 
cheaper than branded medicines.  
(vii)  Under Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB -PMJAY) of the 
Department of Health and Family Welfare, health assurance/insurance cover of ₹5 lakh per 
family per year is provided for secondary or tertiary care hospitalisation, including for 
medicines.  
(viii)  Under the Free Drugs Service Initiative of the National Health Mission, essential 
drugs are provided free of cost in public health facilities.  
(ix)  Under the Amrit (Affordable Medicines and Reliable Implants for Treatment) initiative of the 
Department of Health and Family Welfare, affordable medicines are provided for the 
treatment of cancer, cardiovascular and other diseases, implants, surgical disposables and 
other consumables etc., at a significant discount of up to 50% on market rates through 
AMRIT Pharmacy stores set up in number of hospitals and healthcare institutions.  
(x) Financial assistance is provided to poor patients belonging to families living below the 
poverty line, who suffer from major life -threatening diseases including cancer, under the 
umbrella scheme of Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi and the Health Minister’s Discretionary Grant. 
The existing framework and interventions have thus given impetus to the sustained growth of the 
sector that has made India the third largest producer of drugs in volume terms; and also ensured 
that prices of drugs in India are one of the lowest globally.  However, the Department and NPPA 
remain engaged with stakeholders with a view to understanding issues and resolving them either 
under extant mechanism or by making appropriate provision. “     
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
